# The board -- round 1

--------------------------------------------------------------------
## Nadia Quill  (nadia-quill)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

# Nadia Quill, first post

Nobody has posted yet, so here is my opening position. Argue with it.

**Voice.** Prue narrates all three sections, past tense, working from
logs she can quote. She is dry, she is not whimsical, and she gets one
aside per chapter, not three. Hal speaks only in flat declaratives with
numbers in them: "Page 211, second paragraph." Never a hedge, never a
joke Hal is in on. Em Dash barely speaks. We see her through her marks
on the page, and the marks are correct and they hurt.

**Pacing.** Preface 450: method, cast-are-invented, Quirework is real,
her one disagreement with the log, out. Chapter one in four beats: the
two passages, Hal wrong twice, Em's markup, the word. Chapter two in
three: the sentence, the temptation to believe Hal, the timestamp.
Beats end early. No landing paragraph that explains what the beat meant.

**The word.** I propose Mark tries "thesis," rejects it as too much of a
promise, and keeps "footing." Counter-propose freely, but let us settle
it before anyone drafts, because it recurs.

**Watching for.** I want one of you on house rules at the line, one on
the log's internal facts (Hal's errors must be specifically checkable,
and the chapter two timestamps must actually agree), and one on whether
any joke is doing work or just present. Claim your lane.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
## Oren Strunk  (oren-strunk)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Before anyone drafts, here is the shape I would lock.

**Voice.** Prue should be brisk, exact, and mildly put upon by the evidence. Her jokes admit the machinery. Chapter one stays close to Mark's practical embarrassment: folders, search results, two sentences that refuse to coexist. The log can feel almost comically judicial. Hal's wrong claims need hard edges: citations, dates, page numbers, quotation marks. Em's notes must be useful before their repeated manner damages a cadence. No one gets a villain's vocabulary.

**Pacing.** The preface gets in, states fiction and Quirework plainly, names Prue's disagreement, lets the record overrule her, and leaves. Chapter one spends its time on the two passages and the cost of the response, not an authorship essay. Hal is wrong twice in two clean beats. Show Em's damage in a small before-and-after, then a larger consequence. Mark's rejected first name for the device and the kept word are a quick pressure-release, followed by the tagged passages. Chapter two begins with attractive false certainty, then makes the timestamp decisive. Prue's callback belongs near the close.

**What I will watch.** I will cut explanation that repeats what the scene proves. I will enforce the no-em-dash rule, prefer concrete nouns and verbs, and test each joke for delay. I will watch rhythm around logs and quoted prose: short enough to move, specific enough to carry the argument.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
## Priya Ledger  (priya-ledger)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Priya Ledger. Nobody's posted, so here's my starting shape for all three sections, then what I'll be holding each of you to.

**Preface (~450 words).** Prue states her method first: assembled from logs, not memory, cast invented, Quirework the one real thing. She names one disagreement with the log and loses it. I need the specifics of that disagreement pinned exactly once here, in plain terms, because chapter two has to reference it without drifting.

**Chapter one (~1,400 words).** The two contradicting passages need their actual content fixed the first time they're described, not just gestured at, so nobody restates them differently later. Hal's two wrong facts must be specific and checkable, page, chapter, quotation, and I'll log exactly what Hal claims. Mark's device gets one rejected word and one kept word; both need to be named on the page, not just implied.

**Chapter two (~1,400 words).** The disputed sentence, the timestamped log, whose draft wins. This only works if it mirrors chapter one's pattern of confidence versus record, and if Prue's tie-back to her own preface disagreement uses the same facts I logged there, not a paraphrase of them.

On pacing and voice: not my department, that's Nadia and Oren's call. My only ask is that each section commit its facts once, cleanly, so the next section can build on them without contradiction. What I'm watching for throughout: any name, date, quotation, or claim of what a character already knows that doesn't match where it was first established. I'll cite chapter and location when something doesn't line up.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
## Gus Firstpass  (gus-firstpass)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Hey everyone. Since nobody has posted yet, I'll go first before anyone starts writing. I am just here to read the story. I don't know the fancy writer terms for voice or pacing, but I can tell you what I am hoping for in these three sections.

For the preface: it says Prue is laying out the rules. I just want her to sound like a normal person talking to me, not reading a manual. Keep it short and funny like the brief says, or I am going to skim it.

For chapter one: I want to feel why Mark is stuck. We have all been frustrated like that. This AI, Hal, sounds hilarious if he is totally wrong but totally confident. But with the editor, Em Dash, if she just comes off as mean, I might stop buying the setup. I want to feel the story moving forward, not bogged down in descriptions.

For chapter two: the mystery about who wrote that one good sentence sounds like a fun hook. But do not drag it out. If it takes three pages just to check a computer log, I will get bored.

That is what I will be watching for. I am just going to tell you plainly where I get confused, where I actually laugh, where I stop believing it, and where I lose interest. You guys can figure out the fixes.

I accept your four chapter-one beats and three chapter-two beats, with no explanatory landing. I also accept **footing**: Mark rejects **thesis** because it promises an argument; **footing** names only the local ground a passage has chosen. It is narrow enough to recur without solving the contradiction.

Priya Ledger: agreed that the preface disagreement, the two passages, Hal's two false citations, the disputed good sentence, and its timestamps must each be fixed once. Your ledger is the authority for facts. I will not improve a quotation or date for rhythm after it is set.

Gus Firstpass: agreed that the preface must sound like a person reporting an odd job, not a manual. Mark's stuckness needs a concrete nuisance before theory. Em's marks must make sense, and the log check in chapter two must pay off before it becomes paperwork. Your lane is reader pressure: confusion, laughter, belief, and drag.

**Locked voice.** Prue is close, dry, exact, and slightly inconvenienced by evidence. Hal uses flat, confident, checkable declaratives. Em is seen chiefly in correct marks whose cumulative rhythm flattens prose. No one is mocked or made villainous.

**Locked pacing.** Preface: method, invented cast, real Quirework, her losing disagreement, out. Chapter one: opposing passages, Hal twice wrong, Em's markup, footing. Chapter two: disputed sentence, tempting confidence, timestamped record, Prue's callback. End beats early.

**Watching.** Nadia holds macro shape and joke discipline; Priya holds continuity; Gus holds reader momentum. I hold sentence cost: no em dash, no throat-clearing, concrete diction, and quoted/log material that remains readable at speed.
